sections.heading: a b s t r a c t
sections.text:
Broadband low-frequency vibration and shock energies are ubiquitous such as biomechanical motion, which can be harvested to power wearable electronics. This paper proposes a compact design of V-shaped piezoelectric vibration energy harvester (V-PVEH) with impact stopper. To demonstrate V-PVEH having high power density, Euler beam model is proposed for qualitative comparison between V-PVEH and cantilevered piezoelectric vibration energy harvester (C-PVEH). FEA model in COMSOL for V-PVEH structure design is proposed especially for the stress check. Modal analysis, two bimorphs connection style, tip mass thickness, and acceleration amplitude are discussed in the experimental vibration validation. A peak voltage of $1 1 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ at a low resonant frequency of $1 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and a maximum power of $0 . 4 4 2 \mathrm { \ m W }$ are shown in experiments under the excitation of $0 . 1 \ \mathrm { g } .$ A lumped parameters model with nonlinearity analysis for impact induced broadband and shock input is discussed comprehensively. The stopper design in V-PVEH can not only limit the vibration amplitude and prevent overload, but also form broadband of $8 { - } 1 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ and generate large voltage output of $5 { - } 1 9 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ when impact occurs at an acceleration of $0 . 4 \ \&$ Except for resonating excitation, biomechanical shock energy harvesting with ultra-low frequency of 1 Hz is testified for wearable V-PVEH to charge a $1 0 \mu \mathrm { F }$ capacitor to $1 0 \mathrm { V }$ in 5 s by stamping feet. Above all, V-PVEH with stopper is believed to show good performance in broadband low-frequency vibration and biomechanical shock energy harvesting.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Broadband low-frequency vibration and shock energies are ubiquitous among biomechanical motion [1], vehicle [2], mechanical equipment [3], and other environments. It can be harvested to power wireless sensor nodes [4] and wearable electronics [5] in the booming era of the internet of things (IoT). Piezoelectric vibration energy harvester (PVEH) is a kind of device that resonates under the ambient vibration. Piezoelectric materials produce alternating stress and generate electricity due to the piezoelectric effect [6]. For the practical application, low resonant frequency, broadband, miniaturization, high power density, high reliability, integrable, and other features should be pursued for the PVEH design.

For resonant PVEH, increasing mass and reducing system stiffness are effective means to realize the low-frequency design. To increase the mass in limited design space, Lu Wang [7] adopts an l-shaped mass block. High-density materials, such as tungsten [8], are also very effective for increasing the mass block. At the same time, the reliability of devices should be considered in the design of high quality.

To reduce the stiffness in the limited design space, folded beams [9], zigzag beams [10], spiral beams [11], S-shaped beams [12], Vshaped beams [13] and other piezoelectric beam structures [14] have been studied successively. Besides, the 2 degrees of freedom (DOF) structure can also reduce the resonant frequency of the system [15]. Flexible clamping [16], a combination of a flexible beam and piezoelectric beam [17] can also reduce stiffness effectively.

To enlarge the frequency band of PVEH in the resonant state, broadband approaches have been proposed such as closely multimode design [18], multistability design [19], nonlinearity by magnets [20], nonlinear impact by mechanical stopper [21], and array PVEHs after subsequent circuit processing [22].

Despite the various deformations of beams and the auxiliary settings methods are given in low frequency and broadband design, the utilization ratio of piezoelectric materials [23], and compact structure design [24] need to be considered to achieve a high power density.

Shock excitation is common especially in biomechanical energy harvesting. Besides impact-based piezoelectric design [25,26], resonant PVEH is also suitable in foot biomechanical energy harvesting [27] by shock excitation [28]. The shock response should be optimized and overload protection should be considered.

Overload protection such as a mechanical stopper can avoid stress overload and ensure high reliability [29] of the piezoelectric beam by limiting vibration amplitude [30]. Not only the PZT stress check, but also the nonlinearity analysis of impaction are important in PVEH design.

The combination of the merits above is a challenge in PVEH design. In this study, a V-shaped PVEH with two piezoelectric bimorphs in folded and a proof mass on tip is proposed. Double length of the bimorphs and heavy tip mass ensure the low resonant frequency. Compact design by folding beam in V-shape decrease vibration volume and increase power density. Meanwhile, overload protection design by the tip stopper impact with the root stopper shows broadband characteristics in big acceleration levels.

Although some rectangular folded-beam designs have been reported, they still waste some space in root and middle connectors. What is more, the load of the bottom beam is increased because of the mass of the middle connectors, so that the stress distribution is not synchronized with that of the upper beam. However, a V-shaped folded beam design with small middle connector can perfectly avoid the weakness mentioned above.

Zhao et al. [13] used the distributed parameter model to analyse the multimodal performance with different angular of the V-shape piezoelectric beam. Their design had a big cylindrical middle connector and did not consider the nonlinearity analysis of impact induced broadband and shock response. Finite element analysis (FEA) is more convenient for PVEH design compared to complex distributed parameter model. In most practical applications, the first mode with low resonant frequency is the main concern. The impact induced broadband and biomechanical shock response still need to be discussed by nonlinearity theoretical modeling and experimental validation. Our work will solve these problems by a V-shaped PVEH (V-PVEH) with a stopper impaction design and analysis.

This paper is arranged as follows. Section 1 introduces the necessity and advantages of V-PVEH with stopper design in energy harvesting from broadband low-frequency vibration and shock. Section 2 gives a theoretical analysis and qualitative comparison between the V-PVEH and cantilevered shaped-PVEH (C-PVEH) by Euler beam model. Section 3 gives a low-frequency V-PVEH model and design by FEA model in COMSOL and vibration experimental validation. Eigenfrequency simulation, stress check, modal analysis, voltage response, and optimal load resistance are found for maximum power. The series connection and parallel connection of two piezoelectric bimorphs are discussed. Resonant frequency is tuned by tip mass thickness adjustment. Section 4 builds a lumped parameters (LP) model with nonlinearity analysis for impact induced broadband. Cubic stiffness of impact and acceleration level are discussed and broadband response by the stopper of V-PVEH is tested. Section 5 discusses the performance of V-PVEH with stopper under shock input by simulation in LP model and testifies the application in biomechanical shock energy harvesting by stamping the feet in 1 Hz. Section 6 is the conclusion.

sections.heading: 2.1. PVEH configuration
sections.text:
To demonstrate V-PVEH with a higher power density in low resonant frequency compared with the traditional cantilevered PVEH, three PVEH configurations are presented in this study as shown in Fig. 1a-d. All PVEHs consist of the same tip mass block and the same piezoelectric bimorph with different lengths and configurations. C-PVEH has a cantilevered bimorph with a length of 2 L. V-PVEH has two piezoelectric bimorphs in V-shape folded with a length of L. Cantilevered shaped type 2-PVEH (C2-PVEH) is a piezoelectric cantilever with a length of 1.26L, which is consistent with the resonant frequency of V-PVEH.

The piezoelectric bimorph is composed of a substrate layer in the middle and two piezoelectric layers with the same thickness and the same polarization direction. Here $t _ { p }$ and $t _ { S }$ are the thicknesses of the piezoelectric layer and the substrate layer respectively, $b$ is the width of the bimorph. The surface electrodes of two piezoelectric layers are connected in parallel to improve the piezoelectric output current. Inertial vibration of the PVEHs along the z-axis (transverse with beam) forces the piezoelectric bimorph deformation along the x-axis (longitudinal with beam) to generate electrical power in d31 mode.

sections.heading: 3.1. FEA model and simulation in COMSOL
sections.text:
Although qualitative analysis is done by Euler beam theory to proof the advantages of the V-PVEH structure. For the detailed dynamic model of the V-PVEH, distribute parameter model (DPM) is more accurate [13]. However, complex geometric topologies such as proof mass and connector increase the difficulty of DPM. FEA model is convenient in commercial software such as COMSOL or ANSYS. Therefore, a FEA model of V-PVEH is deployed in COM-SOL for optimizing geometry to match eigenfrequency and check stress. FEA model of V-PVEH in COMSOL is shown in Fig. 2a. Connector $C _ { 1 }$ is fixed and holds one end of the bimorph ${ \sf B } _ { 1 }$ . Connector $C _ { 3 }$ holds one end of the bimorph ${ \sf B } _ { 1 }$ and bimorph ${ \tt B } _ { 2 }$ together to form a Vshape fold. Connector $C _ { 2 }$ holds one end of the bimorph ${ \tt B } _ { 2 }$ , which is bonded with tip proof mass $\mathsf { M } _ { \mathrm { t } }$ . The stopper distance between $C _ { 1 }$ and $C _ { 2 }$ is $d _ { s }$ and limited by stress check. It limits the maximum displacement of the tip proof mass. Here, the angle of C3 is fixed as $1 0 ^ { \circ }$ , and stopper distance can be easily changed by the thickness of ${ \mathsf { C } } _ { 1 }$ and ${ \sf C } _ { 2 }$ . PZT-5H is the piezoelectric material in bimorph, invar steel as the intermediate substrate, copper for the additional mass block, and polylactic acid (PLA) for the connectors. All material parameters are set as the V-PVEH prototype and shown in Table 4. The physical field of solid mechanics is applied in eigenfrequency analysis. Changing the size of proof mass can tune the eigenfrequency of V-PVEH. Fig. 2b shows the first eigenfrequency response curves simulation of V-PVEH with the different mass thickness. Except for the low stiffness by V-shape folded beam, big proof mass also contributes to the low eigenfrequency of V-PVEH. Proper mass thickness design will match with ambient vibration frequency. This research chooses a V-PVEH with the mass thickness of $9 \mathrm { m m }$ in next analysis. Stress check is an essential step in V-PVEH design to limit stopper distance. The gravity of the structure is considered, and tip force is applied vertically downward to the center of the proof mass. Fig. 2c shown the tip amplitude and max stress response curves with the different tip force. The slope of the tip amplitude response curve is the system stiffness. Because PZT has the allowable stress of $8 0 \mathrm { M P a }$ , the allowable safety stress is set as $3 0 \mathrm { M P a }$ in this design to avoid fatigue. The corresponding stopper distance is $5 . 6 \mathrm { { m m } }$ or $4 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ considering the self-weight displacement of $1 . 6 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ when V-PVEH adds a heavy proof mass on the tip with a mass thickness of $9 \mathrm { m m }$ . Multiphysics of electrostatics and electrical circuit are added to analyse the voltage output of the two bimorphs. Removing the tip force and applying the acceleration body load, and piezoelectric effect is considered in frequency analysis. Load resistance of $1 0 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ is connected separately with two bimorphs. Fig. 2d shows the voltage response curves of bimorph 1 and bimorph 2 with the different frequency at an acceleration of $0 . 1 \ \mathrm { g } .$ . The resonate frequency of 12 Hz is a little higher than eigenfrequency of $1 0 . 7 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ because of the electrotechnical coupling. They have almost the same curves due to the little mass of the connector 3.

sections.heading: 3.2. V-PVEH prototype and experimental platform
sections.text:
The test prototype of V-PVEH is shown in Fig. 3a. The connector 1 fix the root of the bimorph 1, connector 2 fix the proof mass in the tip of bimorph 2, and connector 3 fix the bimorph 1 and bimorph 2 as V-shape beam. Bulk PZT layers are fabricated by powder sintering. Connectors are fabricated by 3D printing. The base material is polymer methylate (PMMA) and fabricated by laser cutting. All the parts are bonded by Epoxy resin.

The vibration test platform is shown in Fig. 3b. PC software sets test parameters, including sweep frequency range and vibration amplitude. Vibration controller signals are amplified by a power amplifier (B&K type 2718) and then fed to the exciter (B&K type 4809). The feedback signal is measured by an accelerometer (Delta-Tron type 4519–003). The load resistance of PVEH is adjusted by a resistance decade. Vibration controller (B&K type 7541) also harvests voltage signals in the time domain, which are transformed into frequency domain signals through FFT changes of PC software.

sections.heading: 3.3. Modal analysis of V-PVEH
sections.text:
Sweep frequency test at the acceleration of $0 . 1 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } ( 1 \mathrm { ~ g } = 9 . 8 \mathrm { ~ m } / s ^ { 2 } )$ is utilized in modal analysis of the V-PVEH prototype with a mass thickness of $9 \mathrm { m m }$ . The peak voltage frequency response function (FRF) curves in open circuit state (load resistor $R = 1 0 { \mathrm { M } } \Omega$ ) is shown in Fig. 3c, where B1 represents the voltage of bimorph 1, B2 represents the voltage of bimorph 2, Two summits in FRF curves show two vibration modals of the V-PVEH. A huge summit voltage of 11.5 V occurs in the first resonant frequency of $1 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . Time response curves indicate that bimorph 1 and bimorph 2 have the same voltage phase in the first resonant mode. Bimorph 1 and bimorph 2 have the opposite voltage phase in the second resonant mode with a frequency of $2 5 \mathrm { H z }$ .

Modal shapes of V-PVEH are shown in Fig. 3c. Observing the tip point and the folded point in V-PVEH, they have the same vibration direction in first mode and opposite vibration direction in second mode. Meanwhile, Bimorph 1 and bimorph 2 have the same bending state in first mode and opposite bending state in second mode. Above all, the first resonant mode with large vibration amplitude is the main concern in low-frequency energy harvesting. They can be connected directly in parallel or series without phase difference.

sections.heading: 3.4. Power performance
sections.text:
The variations of voltage and power with load resistance are analysed by a constant frequency excitation test. When V-PVEH with a mass thickness of $9 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ is excited at the acceleration of $_ { 0 . 1 \ g }$ in $1 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , the peak voltage load resistance response curves of two bimorphs in series or parallel are shown in Fig. 3d. Among them, $\mathsf { B } 1 + \mathsf { B } 2$ represents the bimorph 1 (B1) and bimorph 2 (B2) are connected in series, while B1 $I I$ B2 represents the bimorph 1 (B1) and bimorph 2 (B2) are connected in parallel. The parallel open circuit voltage is $1 1 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ as the same of single bimorph open-circuit voltage, and the series open circuit voltage is $2 0 . 6 \mathrm { V }$ , about twice of them.

Fig. 3e shows the root mean square (RMS) power load resistance response curves calculated by $\bar { P } _ { R M S } = \bar { V } _ { P } ^ { 2 } / 2 \bar { R }$ . The peak value of the power curve corresponds to the optimal load resistance. For single B1, the peak power is $0 . 3 7 6 \mathrm { \ m W }$ , the corresponding optimal resistance is $5 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , for single B2, the peak power is 0.385 mW, the corresponding optimal resistance is $6 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . For a parallel connection, the peak power is $0 . 4 4 2 \mathrm { m W }$ , the corresponding optimal resistance is $3 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . For a series connection, the peak power is also $0 . 4 4 2 \mathrm { m W }$ , the corresponding optimal resistance is $1 2 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , which is 4 times bigger than that in parallel connection. Because B2 is in open circuit, B1 is connected to load resistance and absorbs most of the energy. Therefore, the peak power for a single B1 is higher than half of the peak power in series connection or parallel connection.

V-PVEH with a parallel connection of two bimorphs is the main configuration in the next analysis steps. The power density from power $( 0 . 4 4 2 \mathrm { \ m W } )$ divided by vibration volume $\mathbf { \widetilde { 8 . 4 } ~ c m ^ { 3 } = 2 \times 3 }$ $\mathrm { m m } \times 7 0 \mathrm { m m } \times 2 0 \mathrm { m m } )$ is $0 . 0 5 2 6 ~ \mathrm { m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ in $_ { 0 . 1 \ g }$ acceleration at $1 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . Its normalized power density (NPD) is $5 . 2 6 ~ \mathrm { m W } / ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ $\mathrm { g } ^ { 2 }$ ), and normalized volumetric power density (NVPD) is 0.4383 $\mathrm { m } \mathbf { W } / ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } { \cdot } \mathrm { H z } { \cdot } \mathbf { g } ^ { 2 } )$ . This is a considerable power density compared to other cantilevered PVEHs [31] in such low resonant frequency. The performance comparison of various PVEHs is shown in Table 5. To compare the relative bandwidth, $\Delta f / f _ { 0 }$ is the half-power bandwidth divided by resonant frequency, which is also called loss factor for linear vibration system.

sections.heading: 3.5. Resonant frequency adjustment
sections.text: The resonant frequency of the V-PVEH can be tuned by adjusting the thickness of the tip mass. Fig. 3f shows the voltage frequency response curves of V-PVEH with 4 kinds of mass thickness at the acceleration of $_ { 0 . 1 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } }$ . The resonant frequency is decreased and the open-circuit voltage is increased as tip mass thickness increasing. V-PVEH with a heavy tip mass ensures a big voltage output and low resonant frequency.

sections.heading: 4.1. Nonlinearity impact vibration model
sections.text:
V-PVEH with a heavy tip mass would have a large deflection in the resonant state. Stopper design avoids overload and impact occur. The impact induced broadband vibration will be modeled and discussed. Despite FEA model is suitable in complex structure design and analysis, nonlinearity analysis such as impact process is quite difficult to model and solve. It is very intuitive to introduce nonlinear stiffness parameters $K _ { s }$ by lumped parameter (LP) model as shown in Fig. 4a. The displacement excitation of base is $y ( t )$ . The absolute displacement of mass is $x ( t )$ and relative displacement is $z ( t ) = x ( t ) - y ( t )$ . The electromechanical coupling LP model is given in Eq. (5). sections.heading: 4.2. Simulation and experimental validation
sections.text:
Assuming base excitation is $\ddot { y } ( t ) = A s i n \left( \omega t \right)$ , where $A$ is the acceleration level. The voltage frequency response and time response can be simulated by Eq. (5) in MATLAB. Fig. 4b shows the simulation and experimental voltage frequency response curves at $_ { 0 . 1 \ g }$ acceleration. It indicates the LP model can well describe the V-PVEH system. Due to the introduction of nonlinearity, Ode45 (fourth-order to fifth-order Runge Kutta algorithm) time-domain numerical simulation method is applied. Simulation voltage time response curves shown in Fig. 4b indicate the simulation time of 2 s is enough to reach the steady state of the system.

To discuss the effect of cubic stiffness parameters $K _ { s }$ , three kinds of states are discussed in this paper, that is $K _ { s 1 } = 0 N / m ^ { 3 }$ for no stopper, $K _ { s 2 } = 1 0 ^ { 8 } N / m ^ { 3 }$ for soft stopper, and $K _ { s 3 } = 1 0 ^ { 1 0 } N / m ^ { 3 }$ for hard stopper. Fig. 4d shows the simulation nonlinear impact force curves with different cubic stiffness of impact stopper. Considering the influence of self-gravity, stopper distance is set to $3 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ in simulation. Sweeping the frequency from $8 { - } 1 6 \mathrm { H z }$ with the acceleration of $0 . 4 g$ in $2 s$ , the maximum envelope of displacement and voltage frequency response curves are shown in Fig. 4e and f respectively. The impact of stopper induces the peak clipping but broadens the bandwidth on the right side. The harder the stopper, the lower peak clipping, and the wider broadband. The soft stiffness of the stopper can be chosen by adding soft material as stopper layer such as rubber and foam. The stopper distance can be also adjusted by the thickness of the added stopper layer. Here, the hard stopper is chosen in next study.

To study the situation of stopper impaction at different accelerations, simulation and experimental voltage frequency response curves at different acceleration levels are shown in Fig. $_ { 4 g }$ and h respectively. Because the damping will raise with the increase of acceleration levels, a fitting empirical formula for simulation of damping parameters is $D = 0 . 0 8 7 6 +$ $( A - 0 . 1 ) ( 0 . 1 3 - 0 . 0 8 7 6 ) /$ 0.3. In the non-resonant region, the voltage increases linearly with the increase of excitation acceleration. In the resonant region, the peak values are suppressed when excited at larger than the acceleration of $_ { 0 . 2 \ \mathrm { g } }$ . Because connectors 1 and 2 form a stopper distance for amplitude limitation of $3 . 5 ~ \mathrm { { m m } }$ , the maximum peak voltage is limited to $1 9 \mathrm { V } .$ Stopper design not only gives the overload protection but also forms a broadband large voltage output when impact occurs. The right sides of the curves show the nonlinear frequency extension effect in the up-frequency sweep test. And the LP model and simulation are good descriptions of this phenomenon.

The commercial LTC-3588−1 energy harvesting chip has an effective input voltage range of 5 20 V [36]. V-PVEH can realize the effective vibration energy harvesting voltage of $5 { - } 1 9 \mathrm { V }$ at the acceleration of $_ { 0 . 4 \ g }$ in the wide frequency range of $8 { - } 1 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . V-PVEH with LTC-3588 circuit and photograph of lighting up LED are shown in Fig. 4e and f respectively. Standard DC voltage output of $3 . 3 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ is suitable for many consumer electronics such as wireless sensor nodes. Broadband effective input ensures good environmental adaptability.

sections.heading: 5.1. Shock model and biomechanical shock experiment
sections.text:
Except resonant with the sine vibration from ambient excitation, V-PVEH can also harvest shock energy from shock vibration. Assuming the shock base excitation is $\ddot { y } ( t ) = A ( \varepsilon ( t ) - \varepsilon ( t - 0 . 0 1 ) )$ , where $\varepsilon ( t )$ is a unit step function and the shock lasts 0.01 s in simulation. LP model is still used in time domain simulation with the input of shock signal instead of a sinusoidal signal.

Applications in biomechanical shock energy harvesting are shown in Fig. 5a. V-PVEH is mounted on the surface of the shoes. Stamp the feet gently in $1 \mathrm { H z }$ will give a sustained shock stimulation on the V-PVEH. Direct interface circuit means voltage form at parallel connection of two bimorphs, and voltage curves are directly shown on the oscilloscope (keysight DSOX1102 G) with internal load resistance $\mathtt { R _ { L } }$ of $1 \ \mathsf { M } \Omega$ as shown in Fig. 5b. Besides, a standard interface circuit consists of a full bridge (DF10) for rectification and a capacitor ${ \sf C } _ { \sf S }$ for energy storage is shown in Fig. 5c.

sections.heading: 5.2. Different shock acceleration levels
sections.text: V-PVEH with a mass thickness of $9 \mathrm { m m }$ is used here, and shock acceleration level is varied as $2 \ \mathbf { g } , 4 \ \mathbf { g } , 6 \ \mathbf { g }$ and $_ { 8 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } }$ (actually 1.81 $\mathbf { g } , 3 . 6 4 \ \mathbf { g } , 5 . 3 2 \ \mathbf { g }$ and $7 . 2 0 ~ \mathrm { g }$ in experiment), which can cover normal movement of the feet [37]. The negative sign represents the downward shock as stamping of the feet. The simulation results of the shock acceleration input and voltage output are shown in Fig. 6a and b, respectively. The experimental results of the shock acceleration input and voltage output are shown in Fig. 6c and d, respectively. The acceleration input signal is measured by an accelerometer (DeltaTron type 4519–003). Except for the approximate acceleration level and disturbance of raising feet motion in experimental results, the consistency between simulation and experiment results is good. The voltage output amplitude is limited to $2 0 ~ \mathsf { V }$ when shock acceleration input beyond $_ { 4 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } }$ due to the stopper limitation. Decaying wave signal by attenuating free vibration with the resonant frequency of $1 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ is obtained due to electromechanical coupling and mechanical damping.

sections.heading: 5.3. V-PVEH with different mass thickness
sections.text:
To optimize the device for biomechanical energy harvesting, the resonant frequency of V-PVEH should be discussed by tuning the proof mass thickness. Simulation and experimental voltage output of shock energy harvesting by V-PVEH with different mass thickness of $0 \mathrm { m m }$ , $5 \mathrm { m m }$ , and $9 \mathrm { m m }$ at shock acceleration of about $_ { 4 } \mathbf { g }$ are shown in Fig. 7a and b, respectively. Simulation and experimental results both show that V-PVEH with heavy mass has large voltage amplitude with low resonant frequency and slow decay. Periodically stamping the feet in $1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ at shock acceleration of about 4 g, charge curves of $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { F }$ capacitor are also compared in Fig. 7c. Although there is charge leakage in the electrolytic capacitor, $C _ { S }$ of $1 0 \mu \mathrm { F }$ can be charged to $1 0 \mathrm { V }$ in 5 s by V-PVEH with mass thickness of $9 \mathrm { m m }$ . The charging electric power is calculated as $P = C _ { S } U ^ { 2 } / 2 t$ , where $U$ is the capacitor voltage and $t$ is charging time. The average charging electric power of $1 0 \mu \mathrm { F }$ electrolytic capacitor in 5 s is 0.1 mW. ![](images/a06c0f466b05019a01380e49935bcb344404a74026cac61066f34a99d804b4ec.jpg) Fig. 5. V-PVEH with heavy mass has quakily charging speed and large stable voltage due to the large voltage amplitude response in every shock, which indicates a better energy harvesting ability. In the theoretical analysis, the input force will increase with the increase of proof mass at the same acceleration. A high-frequency free vibration is more easily dissipated than a low-frequency free vibration due to the more damping loss. Therefore, the weight of proof mass should be properly chosen. When giving a heavier proof mass, V-PVEH will impact with the stopper, and voltage amplitude response still limited to the $2 0 \mathsf { V } ,$ , which means the extra impact energy will be wasted. Literature review of biomechanical shock energy harvesting in feet is shown in Table 7. Above all, V-PVEH showed good performance in biomechanical shock energy harvesting in foot. The energy storage in the capacitor can be used to power some wireless sensor nodes in the future works.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text:
This paper proposes a V-shape folded piezoelectric energy harvester with impact stopper. Euler beam theoretical analysis and performance comparison show V-PVEH allowable power density is 8 times of C-PVEH power density with the same bimorph length and 1.59 times of C2-PVEH power density with the same eigenfrequency.

The low-frequency V-PVEH is modeled and designed in COM-SOL. A V-PVEH with a mass thickness of $9 \mathrm { m m }$ at parallel connection of B1 and B2 has peak RMS power of $0 . 4 4 2 \mathrm { \ m W }$ in $1 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ resonate frequency and $_ { 0 . 1 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } }$ acceleration by experimental validation.

Impact induced broadband vibration energy harvesting by V-PVEH is also analysed by LP model considering the cubic stiffness by impact force and damping increase with the acceleration level.

V-PVEH also has applications in biomechanical shock energy harvesting. The biomechanical shock by the stamp of the feet in 1 Hz, V-PVEH with the standard interface circuit shows the $0 . 1 \mathrm { m W }$ average charging electric power of $1 0 \mu \mathrm { F }$ to $1 0 \mathrm { V }$ in $5 s$ .

Above all, V-PVEH with stopper is a compact and practical design with good performance in low-frequency broadband vibration and biomechanical shock energy harvesting. It will have great application potential and value in the power of IoT devices by harvesting energy from low vibration and human motion.
